why: Open with the worst moment, then go back to how it began.
example: At 2 a.m. on Diwali night, our payments started failing. Here's how we found out why.

skill.work: On Monday, half our orders failed for an hour. Here's how we found out why.
skill.everyday: My cousin's wedding nearly had no groom. Let me tell you about the traffic.
skill.analogy: Like a film that opens on the car chase, then shows how it started.
skill.insteadOf: So first we did the planning, and then on Monday things started going wrong.

why: Show, in one line, the moment smooth plans met reality.
example: The new office looked perfect, until the first monsoon rain came through the roof.

skill.work: The first week's numbers looked great, until we checked who came back on day seven.
skill.everyday: The trip was going perfectly, until we reached the station and saw our train leaving.
skill.analogy: Like a smooth road that suddenly hits a speed breaker.
skill.insteadOf: The numbers were good, and then after some time they were not so good.

why: Group your points in threes, with the same rhythm. Threes are easy to remember.
example: We cut the load time in half, fixed the top bugs and shipped on time.

skill.work: We fixed the bug, tested it twice and shipped it by Friday.
skill.everyday: We packed the car, picked up Nani and reached Goa by lunch.
skill.analogy: Like masala chai: milk, ginger, sugar. Three things, and you never forget them.
skill.insteadOf: We fixed things and did some testing and other stuff, and then finally we shipped.

why: Turn a big, vague problem into one moment people can picture.
example: Instead of "the app is slow": my mother gave up booking her ticket after four minutes.

skill.work: Instead of saying the form is confusing: one customer tapped sixteen times to download a receipt.
skill.everyday: Instead of saying the hostel was bad: my bucket had a hole, so I bathed in thirty seconds.
skill.analogy: Like a camera zooming from the whole cricket ground to one bowler's face.
skill.insteadOf: The app was really confusing, and users didn't like it.

why: Say the lesson in one line, then stop. Don't let it fizzle out.
example: In the end, the problem wasn't the vendor. It was that nobody asked them first.

skill.work: The lesson wasn't about the code. It was about checking what other teams send us.
skill.everyday: We never found that restaurant. But it was the best street food I've ever had.
skill.analogy: Like a bowler finishing the over and walking off. No extra ball.
skill.insteadOf: So yeah, that's basically it, I guess. Anyway, that's what happened.

why: Owning an early mistake makes the rest of your story easier to believe.
example: I was sure the new intern broke the build. It turned out to be my own change from Friday.

skill.work: We spent two weeks fixing the database before we saw the real problem was the network.
skill.everyday: I blamed the shop for a week before I found the receipt in my own pocket.
skill.analogy: Like a fielder owning the dropped catch before anyone else mentions it.
skill.insteadOf: We found the real problem quickly and solved it.

why: Put the old, painful way next to the new way, so the change is obvious.
example: Last year, getting a refund meant three phone calls and a form. Now it's one tap.

skill.work: Six months ago, adding a new shop took two weeks. Today it takes ninety seconds.
skill.everyday: Last year, Dad couldn't send a photo. This year, he runs the family WhatsApp group.
skill.analogy: Like a before-and-after photo of a messy room.
skill.insteadOf: Adding a new shop is much faster now.

why: Say what we lose if nothing changes, so a small fix feels urgent.
example: It isn't just a late report. If it's not in by Friday, the client can't present on Monday.

skill.work: This isn't only about a slow page. If checkout stays slow, we lose orders in the Diwali sale.
skill.everyday: It wasn't just a flat tyre. If we didn't fix it in an hour, we'd miss my sister's engagement.
skill.analogy: Like a last ball that decides the whole series, not just the match.
skill.insteadOf: We need to fix the page because it's slow.

why: Return to a small detail from the start; the ending feels complete.
example: Remember the shop owner from my first slide? Last night, she ran her whole Diwali sale on our app.

skill.work: Remember the coffee shop owner from the start? Last night, she took her thousandth order on our app.
skill.everyday: And that broken umbrella from the morning? It's now holding up my tomato plants.
skill.analogy: Like a film whose last scene brings back the song from the opening.

why: Add a sound, smell or feeling, so people can picture the moment.
example: It wasn't just a power cut. It was the hum of the generator and the smell of diesel all night.

skill.work: It wasn't just an alert. It was walking into the cold server room at 3 a.m., fans roaring.
skill.everyday: It wasn't just a hot day. My shirt stuck to the auto seat, and the road smelled of tar.
skill.analogy: Like smelling wet earth and suddenly remembering your school's first rainy day.
skill.insteadOf: It was a very stressful night with the servers.

why: Stay silent for a moment before your main line, so people look up.
example: We tried three vendors, two tools and one long weekend. [pause] The fix was a single setting.

skill.work: We checked every part of the system. [pause] The problem wasn't the database. It was our guess.
skill.everyday: We searched the whole house for the keys. [pause] They were in the fridge.
skill.analogy: Like the second of silence before the umpire raises his finger.
skill.insteadOf: We checked everything, and the problem was our guess, not the database.

why: Sharing your honest first doubt helps doubtful listeners relax and hear you out.
example: When my manager asked me to lead the client call, honestly, my first thought was: please, not me.

skill.work: When the team first suggested removing the search bar, honestly, I thought it was a terrible idea.
skill.everyday: When my friends planned a 5 a.m. trek, honestly, I wanted to stay in bed.
skill.analogy: Like a friend admitting he didn't understand the film either. Everyone relaxes and listens.

why: Use the same sentence pattern three times to build pace.
example: We called every vendor. We checked every invoice. We found the mistake by six.

skill.work: We planned it in a morning. We built it in an afternoon. We tested it before dinner.
skill.everyday: We missed the bus. We missed the train. We almost missed the wedding.
skill.analogy: Like a drummer repeating one beat until everyone's feet start moving.

why: Say a big win plainly, without big adjectives. Calm sounds confident.
example: We moved every customer to the new app over one weekend. Nobody noticed. That was the point.

skill.work: Our system handled the whole Diwali sale without a single failure. It was a good Tuesday.
skill.everyday: Mum cooked for forty guests alone and still sat down to eat with us. Not bad for a Sunday.
skill.analogy: Like a batsman reaching a hundred and just raising his bat. No wild celebration.
skill.insteadOf: It was the most amazing, incredible, record-breaking day ever!

why: Share what a person really did or said, not an adjective like "confusing".
example: Instead of "the training went well": three people stayed back an hour to keep asking questions.

skill.work: Instead of calling it confusing: one customer called support in tears because she couldn't find the cancel button.
skill.everyday: Instead of saying Dadi was happy: she danced in the kitchen with a ladle in her hand.
skill.analogy: Like showing the photo instead of describing the view.
skill.insteadOf: The customers found the app very confusing.

why: Explain a technical idea through something everyone does every day.
example: Think of the backup server as a spare tyre: you forget it's there until the day you need it.

skill.work: Our cache is like a waiter who fills your water glass before you ask.
skill.everyday: Saving a little every month is like filling a bucket under a dripping tap.
skill.analogy: Like explaining Wi-Fi to your grandmother as an invisible cable.
skill.insteadOf: The caching layer stores precomputed responses in memory to reduce latency.

why: Give the exact time things changed; it turns an update into a story.
example: At 11:20 on Tuesday, the client said one sentence that changed the project: "What if we start smaller?"

skill.work: At 4:15 on Thursday, we changed one setting, and the errors dropped to zero.
skill.everyday: At 9:40 that night, my phone buzzed once, and the whole trip changed.
skill.analogy: Like the exact ball in a match when everyone knew the game had turned.
skill.insteadOf: At some point, we fixed the problem, and things got better.

why: Pause the story at its most tense point, just before the answer.
example: The demo started in two minutes, and the projector showed nothing but blue. I had one idea left.

skill.work: Fifteen minutes before the market opened, the backup refused to start. We had two options.
skill.everyday: The train doors were closing, my bag was still on the platform, and I had one second to decide.
skill.analogy: Like a TV serial ending the episode just before the big reveal.

move: Slow down for the key line
why: Speak slower and softer just before your most important sentence.
example: Everyone had views on the colours and the logo. Then Priya said quietly, "Our users can't find the pay button."

skill.work: Everyone was arguing about dates. But here's the quiet truth: if we ship this bug, users won't come back.
skill.everyday: Everyone was shouting about the menu. Then Nani said softly, 'Just make sure everyone eats.'
skill.analogy: Like a commentator lowering his voice just before the final ball.

why: Blame the problem, not a team, so people work on it together.
example: The enemy isn't sales or support. It's the three-day wait our customers sit through for a reply.

skill.work: The problem isn't the backend team or marketing. It's the twelve-second load time pushing customers away.
skill.everyday: It's not you against your brother. It's both of you against the messy room.
skill.analogy: Like two rival teams covering the pitch together when the rain comes.
skill.insteadOf: The backend team is slowing us down again.

why: Describe what life looks like once the hard work pays off.
example: Picture next quarter: the reports build themselves, and Friday evenings are ours again.

skill.work: Imagine next Diwali: no late-night calls, no failures, and the whole team home for dinner.
skill.everyday: Imagine next summer: the house painted, the garden green, and all of us on the terrace with chai.
skill.analogy: Like showing the photo of the finished house while you're still laying bricks.

why: Context, problem, fix: three sentences, in under twenty seconds.
example: We moved the team to the new tool on Monday. But half the files wouldn't open. So we kept the old tool running for a week while we fixed them.

skill.work: We launched the new checkout at noon. Sales jumped, but payments failed on slow networks. So we undid one change and fixed it in ten minutes.
skill.everyday: We planned a picnic on Sunday. But it rained all morning. So we ate on the living-room floor, and the kids loved it.
skill.analogy: Like a T20 innings: short, but with a start, a twist and a finish.
skill.insteadOf: We launched, and then there were a few issues, and we did some things, and it's fine now.

why: Start with something that sounds wrong; people lean in to hear why.
example: When we made the sign-up form longer, more people finished it. Here's why.

skill.work: When we raised the price of our premium plan, sign-ups actually went up. Here's why.
skill.everyday: The week I stopped setting an alarm, I started waking up earlier. Let me explain.
skill.analogy: Like a magic trick: something that shouldn't happen makes everyone lean in.

why: Walk through what went wrong, what you learned and what comes next.
example: Last year, we rushed. This year, we slowed down and tested. Next year, we'll do both.

skill.work: Last year, we built fast. This year, we made it stable. Next year, we grow.
skill.everyday: In school, I hated cooking. In college, I lived on instant noodles. Now I cook for the whole family.
skill.analogy: Like three photos of the same plant: a seed, a sapling, a tree.

move: Put the listener in the story
why: Ask listeners to imagine themselves in the main person's place.
example: Imagine you're the new joiner, it's day one, and nobody has given you a laptop.

skill.work: Put yourself in the shoes of an intern who deletes a live database on their first Friday.
skill.everyday: Imagine it's your own wedding, and the caterer calls to say he's stuck in traffic two hours away.
skill.analogy: Like a film that puts the camera behind the hero's eyes.

why: Repeat one short phrase through your talk, so people remember it.
example: Customer first. In design: customer first. In every release: customer first.

skill.work: Clear, not clever. In our code: clear, not clever. In our reports: clear, not clever.
skill.everyday: Dad's rule for every trip: leave early. For trains: leave early. For weddings: leave early.
skill.analogy: Like a song's chorus: you hear it three times and hum it all week.

why: Start with one plain number; it cuts through vague talk.
example: Four out of five support calls this month were about one button. That's what we fix first.

skill.work: Seven in ten mobile users drop off before step two. That's the only number that matters today.
skill.everyday: I spent eleven hours on my phone yesterday. That number is why I'm changing things.
skill.analogy: Like the scoreboard: no speech, just the runs needed.
skill.insteadOf: Our engagement could be improved in a few areas going forward.

why: Make the customer the hero; your product is only their helper.
example: This isn't our story. It's Meena's: she runs a tailoring shop and now sends every bill from her phone.

skill.work: We aren't the heroes here. The hero is the warehouse manager who kept stock records without internet.
skill.everyday: The real hero of our trip wasn't the planner. It was the auto driver who knew every shortcut.
skill.analogy: Like a coach handing the trophy to the players instead of holding it himself.
skill.insteadOf: Our amazing product solved all their problems.

why: Take a common comparison and turn it around, so people listen again.
example: They say a team is a family. I think it's more like a cricket side: everyone has a clear role.

skill.work: People say software is like building a tower. It's more like gardening: skip a week, and the weeds win.
skill.everyday: People say exams are a race. I think they're more like cooking: rush it, and it burns.
skill.analogy: Like turning a well-known saying upside down so people look at it again.

why: Leave a second of silence before and after your key sentence.
example: [pause] We decided to delay the launch by a month, because it wasn't safe yet. [pause]

skill.work: [pause] We said no to the big client, because they wanted us to weaken user privacy. [pause]
skill.everyday: [pause] After twelve years in that house, we finally sold it. [pause]
skill.analogy: Like a frame around a photo: the empty space makes you look at the middle.

why: Share the small, scrappy start; it makes today's result feel earned.
example: This whole training programme began as a ten-minute chat I ran for two new joiners.

skill.work: This payment system started as three lines written on the back of a chai stall receipt.
skill.everyday: Our biggest family tradition began as one cake my aunt baked because the shop was closed.
skill.analogy: Like showing the first small sapling next to today's huge banyan tree.

why: Tell the crisis fast, then slow right down for the fix.
example: Calls coming in, emails piling up, the client on hold. Then Rahul stood up and said, "One at a time."

skill.work: Phones ringing, chats flooding, every dashboard red. And then our senior engineer sat down, took a breath and typed three words.
skill.everyday: The milk boiled over, the doorbell rang, the baby cried. Then Mum turned off the gas and said, 'One thing at a time.'
skill.analogy: Like a train racing through stations, then slowing gently into the last one.

why: Show how a hard limit pushed you to a better solution.
example: Having only two people on the team wasn't a curse. It forced us to cut every feature nobody used.

skill.work: Our tiny cloud budget wasn't a curse. It forced us to build the leanest system in the company.
skill.everyday: Having only one burner in the hostel taught me to cook a whole meal in one pot.
skill.analogy: Like a T20 over limit forcing batsmen to invent new shots.
skill.insteadOf: We had a very small budget, so things were difficult.

why: Quote what a real person said; it brings their problem into the room.
example: I asked a shopkeeper why he still used his notebook. He said, "Because it never asks me for a password."

skill.work: I asked the driver why he didn't use our map. He said, 'Sir, your app kills my battery in twenty minutes.'
skill.everyday: I asked my grandmother why she still writes letters. She said, 'Because you can't keep a phone call.'
skill.analogy: Like hearing the actor's own voice instead of reading the subtitles.
skill.insteadOf: The drivers told us they had some issues with battery usage.

move: Stand still for the big ask
why: Stay still and calm while you make a big recommendation. Calm looks confident.
example: When you ask your manager to let you lead the new project, plant your feet, look at her and say it once.

skill.work: When you recommend closing a product, stand still, look at the decision-maker and say it once.
skill.everyday: When you tell your parents a big decision, sit still, look at them and don't fidget.
skill.analogy: Like a goalkeeper standing still before a penalty: calm looks strong.

why: Share how fixing one problem showed you a second, bigger one.
example: Once we sorted out the late deliveries, we saw the real issue: orders were being entered twice.

skill.work: Once we fixed the slow queries, traffic doubled, and that showed us the payment partner was limiting us.
skill.everyday: Once I fixed the leaking tap, I noticed the real problem: the whole pipe was rusty.
skill.analogy: Like clearing one traffic jam, only to find the next signal is broken.

why: End with one sharp question for people to think about afterwards.
example: If a new customer tried our app today, would they come back tomorrow?

skill.work: If a competitor launched this tomorrow, would we be proud of how fast we respond?
skill.everyday: If your ten-year-old self saw your weekend, would they be happy?
skill.analogy: Like a film that ends on a question, so you discuss it all the way home.
skill.insteadOf: Okay, so that's all from my side. Any questions?

why: Show the patient effort behind a win; it makes success feel reachable.
example: There was no flash of genius. We tried forty versions of the home page before one worked.

skill.work: We didn't have a flash of genius. We tested a hundred and forty models until one beat the old one.
skill.everyday: I didn't suddenly become a good cook. I burnt about fifty rotis first.
skill.analogy: Like a batsman's hundred built on years of nets practice, not one lucky day.
skill.insteadOf: We had a brilliant idea, and it worked.

why: Mix short, punchy lines with one longer sentence to keep the rhythm alive.
example: The call dropped. Twice. Then, just as the client unmuted to say yes, the power went out in the whole building.

skill.work: It failed. We regrouped. Then we rewrote the whole module over three long nights in the Bengaluru office.
skill.everyday: It rained. We waited. Then we ran, laughing, through the flooded street to the only open chai stall.
skill.analogy: Like a bowler mixing short, fast balls with one slow, looping delivery.

why: End by inviting the listeners to own what happens next.
example: The plan is ready, and the tools are in place. Who picks up the first task on Monday?

skill.work: The base is ready and tested. What we build on it this year is in all our hands.
skill.everyday: Dadi's recipes are all written down now. Who cooks them next Diwali is up to us.
skill.analogy: Like a relay runner handing the baton to the next runner.
